items.title: [FDD Diary #004] The Real Problem
content:
Not the AI's fault.
Not the prompt's fault.

The problem was deeper.

I didn't know what I was building.

FDD Diary #004 🧵

"Connect three computers."
That's a wish, not a design.

Monday: "File sync first."
Wednesday: "Screen sharing first."
Friday: "Remote commands first."

Direction changed every time.
AI built in that direction every time.
Every time convincing. Every time different.

AI doesn't say "Hey, last week we were doing file sync.
Why suddenly screen sharing?"

It just follows orders. Silently.

I can't read code.
So every time, AI built from scratch.
The same thing. A different way. Five times.

Implementation is free.
Claude makes files. Functions. Tests. Bug fixes.
All free.

But deciding what to build?
That's not free. AI can't do that.
Only you can.

"What if I just write better prompts?"

No. Prompts weren't the problem.
There was no destination.

The taxi just kept driving in circles.

items.title: [FDD Diary #005] Frustration Is the Spec
content:
They said I need to write a spec.

Spec? Like phone specs?
RAM, storage, screen resolution?

I'm not a developer.
Never opened a document and typed "1. System Overview."

FDD Diary #005 🧵

Searched for how to write specs.
SRS. PRD. Functional specs.
All developer documents.

"Non-functional requirements" — what?
"System constraints" — what?

I started vibe coding because I didn't want to learn coding.
Now you're telling me to learn spec writing?

So I just got pissed.

Asked AI.
"Can I connect three computers directly?"
"P2P is possible. Behind NAT, tricky."
"What's NAT?"
"Behind a router."
"How do you connect behind a router?"
"QUIC tunnels or STUN/TURN servers."

Every "no" became a condition.

I got pissed. Asked questions. Fought. Organized.

And the spec was already there.

Purpose: Multiple computers as one.
Reason: Nothing works. Everything half-assed.
Method: Direct P2P. QUIC tunnels.
Means: Open-source. MIT verified.

Four things. That's a spec.

It doesn't come from a whiteboard in a conference room.
It comes from "why the hell doesn't this work."

Frustration is the Spec.

items.title: [FDD Diary #006] Everything Changed
content:
Once I had the spec, everything changed.

Day one.
AI tried to install a cloud SDK.
Showed it the spec.
"It says no cloud. Right there."

For the first time, the AI was following MY spec.

FDD Diary #006 🧵

And I could delete things.
For the first time, I could actually delete code.

Opened the ten-thousand-line codebase.
Found something not in the spec. Deleted it.
Found another. Deleted that too.

Three thousand lines left.
App didn't break. It got faster.

Forty-five minutes became twelve.
Switched Python to Rust. Even faster.
Failure rate dropped from 30% to 3%.

Seven thousand lines gone.
Nothing broke.

Because now I knew what was supposed to be there.

But reality doesn't follow specs perfectly.

Got punched. Fixed it. Wrote it down.

Made a file called PROBLEMS.md.
Every time something breaks, write it down.
One week later, same problem.
Opened the file. Fixed in five seconds.

Specs are living documents.

Better prompts aren't the answer.
Better AI tools aren't the answer.
Knowing what you're building is the answer.

Specs don't come from conference rooms.
They come from the grind.
